issues.legal_issue: A refusal to readmit a first appeal dismissed for nonappearance is challengeable by an appeal to the High Court, rather than by a supervisory writ petition.
material_facts: A first appeal was dismissed in default when the appellant’s counsel did not appear for the hearing.
The appellant applied to have the appeal restored, but the appellate court dismissed that application.
The appellant challenged the refusal by a writ petition under Article 227, which the High Court dismissed.
issues.conclusion: The refusal to readmit the appeal was appealable to the High Court under Order 43 Rule 1(t) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court should have declined to entertain the writ petition and, in its discretion, converted it into an appeal or permitted its withdrawal with liberty to appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41 Rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure governs readmission of an appeal dismissed for default, subject to sufficient cause for nonappearance. An order refusing readmission under that rule is expressly appealable under Order 43 Rule 1(t); the appropriate remedy is therefore a statutory appeal, not a petition under Article 227 of the Constitution.

predicates.first_appeal_dismissed_for_nonappearance: A party’s first appeal was dismissed after that party or its representative failed to appear when it was called for hearing.
predicates.restoration_request_refused: The appellate court refused the party’s request to restore the appeal.

issues.definition: When a first appeal is dismissed for nonappearance and the request to restore it is refused, the refusal order is challengeable by appeal.

issues.legal_issue: A first appeal dismissed without a hearing on the merits should be restored when the application establishes sufficient cause for nonappearance, with terms available to address prejudice to the opposing party.
material_facts: The appellant’s first appeal from a decree was dismissed in default because its counsel did not appear when the appeal was called for hearing.
The appellant applied for recall of the dismissal order and restoration of the appeal.
The Supreme Court found that the restoration application established sufficient cause under Order 41 Rule 19.
The dismissal was in default, not on the merits, and the appeal was a valuable right to be heard on its merits.
The Court conditioned restoration on payment of costs to the respondent.
issues.conclusion: The restoration application was allowed and the first appeal was restored for hearing on the merits, subject to payment of costs to the respondent.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41 Rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits readmission of an appeal dismissed for default where sufficient cause prevented the appellant from appearing. As explained in Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal, Kotah, AIR 1955 SC 425, procedural rules should be applied to facilitate justice and consistently with natural justice, rather than used to deprive a litigant of participation when a fair remedy, such as costs, can address prejudice to the other side.

predicates.first_appeal_dismissed_without_merits: A party’s first appeal was dismissed without the court hearing or deciding its merits.
predicates.appellant_failed_to_appear: The appellant or its representative did not appear when the first appeal was called for hearing.
predicates.restoration_application_shows_sufficient: The appellant’s application establishes a sufficient reason for the failure to appear.
predicates.appeal_restored_on_just_terms: The dismissed appeal is restored for a hearing on its merits, subject to appropriate terms addressing prejudice to the opposing party.

issues.definition: When a first appeal is dismissed without a merits hearing because the appellant failed to appear, and the restoration application shows sufficient cause, the appeal is restored on just terms.
